name: Chico (sapodilla)
summary: This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant chico from a marcot or a grafted seedling and care for it until the first fruits. It is for backyards and small orchards, mostly with the common Pineras and the big fruited Ponderosa.
season: Marcots and grafted seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July. Chico stands drier places better than most fruit trees, and in the Philippines it flowers most around April to June, with the main harvest about December to February.
material: In the old way growers make their own marcots: in the rainy season they girdle a fairly upright branch about 1 cm thick on a good bearing tree, wrap it in moist coir or soil and plastic, and cut it once roots fill the wrap, which can take 4 to 12 months. Many nurseries now sell cleft grafted seedlings on seedling rootstock. Trees from seed are slow to bear and many give poor crops.
spacing: About 6 to 10 m between trees, one plant a hole. Some growers use about 9 m between rows and 6 to 7 m in the row. Planting two varieties near each other helps fruit set, since some kinds need pollen from another tree.
water: Mostly rain fed. New trees are watered in dry spells until they take hold. Bearing trees in dry places do better with water during flowering and fruit growth, since flowers and young fruits drop when the soil is too dry.
fertilizer: Compost or manure in the hole. Young trees get a little complete fertilizer or manure at the start and again before the end of the rains, more each year. Grown trees need a lot of nitrogen with some phosphorus and potash, spread in a ring under the edge of the canopy at the same two times.
care: Staking and mulching young trees, weeding a circle around them, very light pruning, removing sagging low branches, and checking for mealybugs, scale and fruit borers. Bees help set fruit, so growers avoid harming them.
harvest: Fruits take about 6 to 8 months from flowering to maturity, and the main crop in the Philippines comes about December to February. Mature fruits are yellowish brown, the brown bloom rubs off easily, and little sap flows when the fruit is pulled off. Growers test a few first. After picking, the fruits are soaked so the sap bleeds out, scrubbed, dried stalk end down and left to ripen in 3 to 7 days.

ways.label: Marcot or grafted seedling (marcot o grafted)

steps.title: Make the marcot
steps.how: In the rainy season, pick a healthy, fairly upright branch about 1 cm thick on a heavy bearing tree. Peel a ring of bark, wrap the cut with moist coir or soil in plastic and tie both ends.

parts.title: Choose the mother tree and the branch
parts.how: Pick a tree that bears every year, with good fruit and no pests or disease, and not too old. On it choose a branch about 1 cm thick, neither too young nor too old, growing upward in the sun, with no flowers or fruit on it.

parts.title: Mix the rooting ball
parts.how: Mix garden soil with rice hull, or with mudpress from a sugar mill or coir dust where you can get it. Wet it until it holds together when squeezed but does not drip.

parts.title: Peel a ring of bark
parts.how: With a clean, sharp knife, cut twice around the branch a short distance apart and peel off the bark between the cuts. Scrape off the slippery green layer under the bark too, or the bark heals over instead of making roots.

parts.title: Wrap and tie
parts.how: Hold a piece of clear plastic around the branch below the ring, pack a ball of the moist mix over the whole ring, close the plastic around it and tie both ends tightly with plastic straw.

parts.title: Wait for the roots
parts.how: Chico roots slowly. Leave the wrap on the tree and look at it every few weeks, adding a little water at the top if the ball dries. It is ready when roots fill the ball and show all around through the plastic.

steps.title: Cut and pot the rooted marcot
steps.how: When roots show all through the wrap, cut the branch below it, remove the plastic and plant it in a bag of loose soil. Keep it in light shade and water it until new leaves come.

parts.title: Cut it and bag it
parts.how: Cut the branch just below the ball with sharp shears or a saw. Take off the plastic gently, without breaking the ball, and plant it in a 6 by 8 inch bag of two parts soil, one part compost and one part rice hull.

parts.title: Nurse it in the shade
parts.how: Keep the new plant in the shade, out of the rain, and water it daily. After two weeks move it where it gets some sun, and pick off any flowers so it grows roots and leaves first.

steps.title: Mark and dig the holes
steps.how: Mark the planting spots about 6 to 10 m apart, wider for big trees. Dig holes wider than the bag and mix the topsoil with compost or manure for filling back.

steps.title: Plant at the start of the rains
steps.how: Remove the bag without breaking the soil ball and set the plant at the same depth. Fill in, press the soil, water well and tie the young tree to a stake against wind.

steps.title: Water in dry spells
steps.how: Water the new tree whenever a dry spell comes until it is well rooted, and mulch around the base. Shade it lightly for the first weeks if the sun is harsh.

steps.title: Weed and give the first feeding
steps.how: Keep a clean circle around the tree and give it a little complete fertilizer or manure, spread in a ring and covered. Feed at the start and again before the end of the rains each year, more as it grows.

steps.title: Check for pests
steps.how: Look at new shoots and fruits for mealybugs, scale insects and fruit borers, and cut off and burn badly hit twigs. Keep fallen leaves and fruit cleaned up.

steps.title: Light shaping only
steps.how: Chico needs little pruning since flowers come near the shoot tips. On upright trees cut back the main leader early so side branches form, and later remove low branches that touch the ground.

steps.title: First fruits
steps.how: Pick when the skin turns from green to yellowish brown, the brown powder rubs off easily with the thumb and little sap flows when the fruit is pulled off. Soak the fruits in water so the sap bleeds out, scrub off the powder and let them ripen in 3 to 7 days.

ways.note: Marcotted chico usually starts bearing at about 3 to 4 years and grafted trees at about 4 to 6 years. Fruits take about 6 to 8 months from flowering to maturity.

mistakes: Planting seedlings from seed, which take many years and often bear poorly.
Picking fruits that are still green under the bloom, so they never ripen sweet.
Skipping the soak after picking, so sap hardens inside the fruit.
Pruning hard, which cuts off the shoot tips where flowers form.
Planting a lone Ponderosa tree with no other variety nearby for pollen.
Letting young trees dry out in their first dry season.
better: Use marcots or grafted seedlings from a proven, heavy bearing tree or an accredited nursery.
Test the soil and feed by the result, twice a year at the start and end of the rains.
Water during flowering and fruit growth in dry places to stop flower and fruit drop.
Plant two or more varieties near each other for better fruit set.
Scout for mealybugs, scale and fruit borers and clean up fallen fruit.
Sort and bleed the fruits right after picking for a better price.
